relationships.notes: SE01 buys from SE02 across three categories. First, steel for drilling and pipeline construction. Second, specialty materials including specialty chemicals for refinery operations and copper and aluminium for energy transmission equipment and renewable infrastructure. Third, silver for solar cell manufacturing — silver paste is technically non-substitutable in current solar photovoltaic cell designs. Solar PV has become silvers largest and fastest-growing industrial end-use globally, and supply disruption in silver directly raises solar panel manufacturing costs. This silver dependency applies only to SE01 solar sub-industry. The overall dependency is medium because SE01 long-lived assets mean materials procurement is intensive at capex phases but not a continuous operational input.

SE01 has a deep and structural dependency on SE03 for both oilfield services and EPC construction. Oilfield services provide drilling rigs, well services, subsea equipment, offshore installation vessels, and EPC fabrication for upstream operations. Renewable energy project development requires civil construction and EPC services for utility-scale solar and wind farms. Power plant EPC for conventional generation is also procured from SE03. This dependency is high because upstream exploration and production cannot physically occur without these services.

SE05 sugar sub-industry and grain processors co-produce ethanol as a biofuel feedstock sold to SE01 oil marketing companies for blending into petrol and diesel. Sugar mills produce ethanol from sugarcane molasses, sugarcane juice, and damaged grain. This dual-output structure means SE05 is simultaneously a food producer and a bioenergy feedstock supplier to SE01. The relationship is structurally present across major sugarcane-producing EM geographies: Brazil operates the world largest sugarcane ethanol programme; India has an active ethanol blending programme; Indonesia and Thailand operate palm-based biodiesel blending programmes. Medium strength — the biofuel programme is policy-mandated but procurement volume is bounded by blending targets and sugar mill production decisions.

SE01 is among the most capital-intensive sectors across both fossil and renewable segments in every EM geography. Upstream E&P requires project finance for exploration and development. Renewable energy IPPs depend almost entirely on long-term project finance loans, green bonds, and DFI funding — multilateral DFIs (IFC, ADB, AIIB) and national DFIs are the largest providers of clean energy project finance across EM markets. Without access to institutional capital from SE07, SE01 capacity expansion programme cannot proceed at the scale that energy security requirements demand.

SE01 buys IT services, AI platforms, and digital infrastructure from SE08 across its operations. In upstream: AI-guided drilling optimisation, predictive maintenance for rigs and pipelines, subsurface data analysis using generative AI, digital twin technologies. In midstream and downstream: SCADA and Distribution Management Systems. In renewable energy: smart grid software, energy management systems, grid integration analytics. The dependency is medium — IT enhances operational efficiency but physical energy infrastructure can operate suboptimally without it.

SE01 oil, gas, and energy companies buy connectivity from SE09 for operational monitoring and digital field management. Upstream operations use satellite and cellular connectivity for remote well monitoring, pipeline telemetry (leak detection, pressure monitoring), and offshore platform communications. LNG terminals and gas pipelines use SCADA over cellular and fibre for operational control. Renewable energy site monitoring in remote locations depends on cellular connectivity for generation data, inverter telemetry, and grid feed management. Medium strength — SE01 physical energy production can continue without real-time connectivity, but safety monitoring, remote operations, and regulatory compliance increasingly require it.

SE01 IG0103 renewable energy equipment manufacturers (solar PV module factories, wind turbine component manufacturers) are electricity-intensive industrial operations that buy grid electricity from SE10 as a primary operational input. Solar module manufacturing involves energy-intensive processes — silicon purification and ingot growth, wire-saw wafering, cell diffusion and passivation, silver paste screen printing, and lamination are all powered by industrial electricity. A grid electricity tariff increase for industrial users directly raises the production cost of solar modules and wind equipment, which flows through to the levelised cost of renewable energy projects. Medium strength — SE01 equipment manufacturers can partly offset grid electricity costs through captive solar or open-access renewable procurement, but grid tariff is the primary short-term baseline.

SE01 depends on SE12 across two structurally distinct categories. First, physical transport infrastructure for commodity flows — SE01 upstream oil and gas, LNG import, and coal import sub-industries depend structurally on SE12 port infrastructure for import of crude oil, LNG, thermal coal, and export of petroleum products. A port disruption directly halts crude oil supply to refineries — a non-substitutable, structurally high dependency. SE01 coal sub-sector uses rail freight infrastructure for moving domestic coal from mines to power plants. Second, infrastructure investment vehicles for capital recycling — SE01 renewable energy IPPs increasingly use InvIT structures to monetise operational renewable energy assets and recycle capital for greenfield project development.

SE02 buys from SE01 across two distinct dependency types. First, energy — thermal coal and natural gas are primary fuel inputs for steelmaking furnaces, cement kilns, and chemical plant operations. Coking coal (blast furnace reductant) is classified within SE02 own steel sub-industry, NOT as an SE01 product — this distinction is locked in the taxonomy. Second, raw material feedstock — crude oil derivatives (naphtha, LPG, ethane) from SE01 downstream refining are the primary chemical feedstock for petrochemical cracking into ethylene, propylene, and polymers. Fertiliser production uses natural gas both as energy and as hydrogen feedstock for ammonia synthesis. The thermal coal and gas dependency is structural and non-substitutable; disruption in SE01 thermal fuel supply directly impairs SE02 production capacity.

SE02 buys two categories of inputs from SE03. First, capital equipment — mining equipment (excavators, haul trucks, conveyor systems, mineral processing equipment) for iron ore, coal, bauxite, and copper mining operations; heavy engineering equipment for steel plants; plant and machinery for chemical facilities. Second, EPC services — specialist EPC contractors provide turnkey construction and commissioning of steel complexes, aluminium smelters, cement plants, and chemical manufacturing facilities across all EM geographies. Mining equipment is procured infrequently (long asset lives) making this medium rather than high strength, but it is essential for capacity expansion and greenfield projects.

SE02 is among the most capital-intensive sectors in every EM geography. Greenfield steel plants, integrated aluminium complexes, cement expansions, and large chemical facilities require project finance structured over long tenors through banks, development finance institutions, and bond markets. Working capital facilities are also significant — chemicals companies require substantial revolving credit for feedstock procurement and receivables financing. The capital dependency is pervasive and existential: without access to institutional finance, capacity expansion in SE02 cannot occur at the scale that industrial development requires.

SE02 heavy industries buy AI and digital transformation services from SE08 to optimise production efficiency and reduce input costs. AI/ML platforms are deployed for blast furnace optimisation, predictive maintenance for smelters and chemical plants, digital twins for process simulation and material consumption optimisation, integrated control centre systems for steel and mining operations, and ERP for procurement and supply chain management. Medium strength — the physical production processes can operate suboptimally without it; the dependency is strategic and growing but not yet production-stopping.

SE02 materials industries (mining, steel, chemicals, cement) buy enterprise connectivity from SE09 for industrial IoT and operational monitoring. Mining operations use IoT sensors and cellular connectivity for real-time ore grade monitoring, equipment telemetry, and autonomous mining vehicles. Steel mills and chemical plants deploy IoT sensors over cellular networks for process monitoring, predictive maintenance, and energy management. Connectivity enables remote monitoring of geographically dispersed mining sites and chemical plants in EM markets. Medium strength — SE02 physical production can continue without IoT connectivity but at higher operating cost and lower efficiency.

SE02 is among the most electricity-intensive sectors in the economy. Aluminium smelting (electrolytic process), electric arc furnace steelmaking, chlor-alkali chemical production, and industrial gas separation are all electrically-driven or highly electricity-dependent processes. Power costs are a primary line item in SE02 cost structures — electricity disruption directly impairs production capacity. Industrial manufacturing is the single largest end-use category of electricity, with SE02 energy-intensive processes accounting for a structurally significant share of that consumption.

SE02 heavy industries depend on SE12 transport infrastructure as the primary physical network for raw material inbound logistics and product outbound logistics. Iron ore, coking coal, and limestone move from mines to steel plants via rail freight and road transport. Aluminium bauxite is bulk-shipped via ports. Chemicals are moved by road tankers, rail, and coastal shipping. Export-oriented SE02 companies depend on SE12 port access for product exports. In EM markets with incomplete logistics infrastructure, SE12 capacity constraints directly limit SE02 industrial output — a mine with no rail connection to a port cannot achieve commercial viability.

SE03 Industrials — manufacturing, logistics, construction, transport — is a major buyer of refined petroleum products (diesel for construction equipment, generators, logistics fleets), coal and gas (for industrial process heat and industrial boilers). Diesel is the primary fuel for freight and construction activity. Industrial gas (LPG/PNG and increasingly LNG) powers industrial processes — in many EM geographies, industrial natural gas arrives as LNG via SE12 port infrastructure before reaching industrial buyers, creating a second-order SE12 port dependency embedded within the SE01 to SE03 energy relationship. The dependency is high because physical construction, mining equipment operation, and freight logistics cannot function without refined petroleum fuel inputs.

SE03 capital goods manufacturers, engineering companies, and transport/logistics operators buy from SE02 across three categories. First, structural metals — steel is the dominant physical input for heavy engineering, capital goods, industrial machinery, electrical equipment, and defence equipment manufacturing; aluminium and copper are used in electrical equipment, cables, and heat exchangers. Second, specialty chemicals — coatings, adhesives, industrial lubricants, and industrial gases from SE02 are process inputs for SE03 manufacturing operations. Third, synthetic rubber and polymers — SE03 transport and logistics fleet depends on synthetic rubber and engineering polymers from SE02 Petrochemicals and Polymers sub-industry; tyre manufacturers serving the logistics and construction fleet are direct buyers of synthetic rubber; seals and gaskets for industrial machinery require specialty polymers.

SE03 has two distinct financial dependencies on SE07. First, project finance and working capital — defence MSMEs and startups require working capital credit and MSME loans; capital goods manufacturers require working capital for long production cycles; EPC contractors require bid bonds, performance guarantees, and construction finance for large infrastructure contracts. These are universal financial service requirements for industrials companies across all EM geographies. Second, aircraft leasing — airlines across EM markets depend heavily on aircraft lessors for fleet financing, as purchasing aircraft outright is capital-prohibitive for most carriers; aircraft leasing is the dominant fleet acquisition model globally.

SE03 Industrials buys IT services, AI platforms, and digital tools from SE08 across three sub-sectors. First, logistics and supply chain — logistics operators buy TMS, WMS, IoT fleet tracking, route optimisation algorithms, and AI demand forecasting platforms from SE08. Second, manufacturing — capital goods and engineering manufacturers buy MES, ERP, predictive maintenance platforms, and industrial automation software. Third, EPC and construction — project management software, BIM, drone survey platforms, and digital twin systems for complex infrastructure projects. The dependency is medium — industrial operations can function without advanced IT but efficiency and competitiveness are materially impaired.

SE03 buys connectivity from SE09 across logistics and manufacturing applications. Logistics and freight operators depend on mobile connectivity for real-time fleet tracking, warehouse management systems, proof-of-delivery applications, and cold chain temperature monitoring over IoT. Manufacturing companies buy enterprise 5G connectivity (private networks, network slices) from telecom operators for Industry 4.0 applications — IoT sensor networks, predictive maintenance, autonomous guided vehicles, and real-time quality control. Medium strength — logistics and manufacturing operations can function without advanced connectivity but at significantly lower efficiency.

SE03 industrial manufacturing, logistics, and construction operations buy electricity from SE10 as a primary operational input. Manufacturing plants are electricity-intensive — production lines, machining centres, conveyor systems, and compressed air systems all require continuous grid power. Logistics and warehousing operations require electricity for handling equipment, lighting, cold storage, and office systems. Grid electricity is non-substitutable for continuous manufacturing operations — a prolonged power outage halts production with immediate revenue impact. High strength — SE03 manufacturing cannot operate without continuous electricity; the dependency is structural and universal across all EM geographies.

SE03 buys real estate from SE11 across two structurally distinct categories. First, logistics park and warehousing real estate — SE03 3PL logistics operators are the single largest tenant category in Grade A industrial and logistics real estate; 3PL operators lease multi-user warehousing facilities and specialised distribution centres from SE11 Warehousing and Logistics Parks developers. The 3PL business model depends entirely on leased logistics real estate — 3PL companies do not own the physical warehouses they operate. Second, airport commercial real estate — SE03 aviation sub-industries require terminal buildings, cargo handling areas, and commercial zone space within airport campuses. Medium strength overall — 3PL leasing is operationally essential but logistics park supply is growing across EM geographies, reducing short-term scarcity risk.

SE03 logistics operators depend on SE12 transport infrastructure as the physical network over which freight movement occurs. Road freight uses national highways and expressways. Port access enables import/export cargo handling. Rail freight moves SE03 bulk and containerised freight. Air cargo operators access SE12 airport infrastructure. Without SE12 infrastructure, SE03 logistics operations cannot physically move goods. High strength — logistics is physically impossible without transport infrastructure; SE03 is the primary commercial user of SE12 infrastructure assets, and the economic viability of SE03 logistics businesses is directly linked to infrastructure quality and capacity.
MSME manufacturers across SE03 sub-industries procure working capital credit and term loans from commercial banks through Mudra/CGTMSE frameworks and direct MSME lending schemes.

MSME manufacturing units across SE03 sub-industries procure equipment on hire purchase and leasing arrangements from NBFC equipment financiers as their primary capital goods acquisition mechanism; NBFCs specialise in asset-backed equipment lending at MSME scale where commercial bank credit structures are not suited to short-tenor, collateralised lending. This is a capital procurement — NBFC equipment hire purchase and leasing is a financial capital relationship; MSMEs access equipment through financial arrangements rather than outright cash purchase.

MSME manufacturers across SE03 use UPI and digital payment infrastructure for B2B payment collection from buyers, payroll disbursement, and supplier payment — digital payment rails enable MSMEs to participate in formal commerce and supply chains. This is an infrastructure procurement — digital payment access is a non-substitutable operational dependency for MSME formal sector participation.

SE04 has two primary fuel dependencies on SE01. First, automotive fuel — petrol for personal vehicles and two-wheelers, diesel for commercial vehicles, aviation turbine fuel for airlines, CNG for CNG-fitted vehicles via city gas distribution networks. Petrol and diesel consumption grows with vehicle ownership penetration across EM markets. Second, gas-based transport fuels — CNG is a significant transport fuel across multiple EM geographies: China is the largest CNG vehicle market globally, followed by Iran, Brazil, Argentina, India, Egypt, and Pakistan where natural gas pricing relative to petrol incentivises adoption; LPG vehicle conversions are widespread in Southeast Asia and Latin America.

SE04 has four distinct sub-dependencies on SE02. First, automotive — flat-rolled steel is the primary structural material for vehicle bodies and chassis; aluminium for lightweighting; critical minerals and REEs are non-substitutable inputs for EV motors; lithium is the primary electrochemical input for EV battery cells with China dominating lithium refining. Without REEs and lithium, manufacturing an EV is structurally impossible. Second, textiles — polyester, nylon, viscose, and acrylic synthetic fibres are petrochemical derivatives from SE02 used as primary raw material alongside natural cotton. Third, packaging and consumer electronics — e-commerce is a fast-growing buyer of flexible and protective packaging materials from SE02. Fourth, gems and jewellery — jewellery manufacturers and retailers buy refined gold bullion and diamonds from SE02 as primary raw material inputs.

SE04 buys logistics and transport services from SE03 across two critical sub-dependencies. First, e-commerce and retail logistics — the e-commerce sector depends fundamentally on SE03 freight and logistics sub-industries for last-mile delivery. Quick commerce platforms operate dense dark store networks with same-day or sub-hour delivery cycles — this is among the most logistics-intensive commercial models in the economy. E-commerce without logistics is structurally impossible. Second, aviation linkage to hospitality — domestic aviation network expansion is a structural demand driver for hotels and hospitality in cities that gain new air connections; new routes create economically viable hotel markets in destinations that previously lacked sufficient visitor volumes.

SE04 buys from SE05 across two structurally distinct categories. First, cotton and natural fibres as raw material — SE04 textiles sub-industry is directly dependent on SE05 agricultural production for natural fibre inputs. Cotton is the primary natural textile fibre in major EM geographies. Natural fibre supply disruption (drought, pest infestation, policy export restrictions) directly impairs mill operations. Second, FMCG product inventory — SE04 retail sub-industries stock and sell SE05 consumer staples products (packaged foods, beverages, dairy, household products, personal care) as the primary inventory category. This is SE05 primary domestic distribution channel — the route through which consumer staples products reach end households.

SE04 retail sub-industries buy OTC medicines, consumer health products, nutraceuticals, vitamins, and wellness brands from SE06 Consumer Health and OTC sub-industries for resale to end consumers. This is the primary route-to-market for SE06 consumer health products — the retail channel is how OTC and wellness products reach the end consumer. SE04 retailers stock these products as a category alongside FMCG goods, using the same shelf space, distribution networks, and trade channels. Medium strength — SE04 retailers do not depend structurally on SE06 OTC products to operate; the dependency direction is primarily SE06 route-to-market depending on SE04 retail channels.

SE04 has two strong financial dependencies on SE07. First, consumer credit — auto loans finance passenger vehicle and two-wheeler purchases across all EM geographies; vehicle loan growth directly tracks automotive sales. NBFC and consumer finance company CV financing enables commercial vehicle purchases. BNPL and digital credit enables consumer electronics and e-commerce purchases. Second, motor insurance — motor own-damage and third-party liability insurance is a mandatory product for every registered vehicle in most EM geographies; motor insurance volumes are structurally correlated with vehicle registration volumes. Without auto finance and motor insurance, automotive demand would be significantly lower — both are structural enablers of vehicle ownership and usage across all EM markets.

SE04 buys from SE08 across two categories. First, digital services — retail and e-commerce companies buy AI-powered recommendation engines, personalisation platforms, demand forecasting algorithms, last-mile route optimisation, and digital payment platform integrations from SE08. E-commerce is structurally IT-dependent — every transaction flows through SE08-built platforms. Second, ESDM components — automotive OEMs and two-wheeler manufacturers buy electronics, automotive-grade PCBs, engine control units, EV power electronics, ADAS components, and infotainment systems from SE08 ESDM sub-industry. High strength overall — e-commerce cannot function without digital infrastructure; automotive electronics content per vehicle is structurally rising with EV and ADAS penetration.

SE04 has two distinct connectivity dependencies on SE09. First, e-commerce and digital retail — every e-commerce transaction is delivered over SE09 mobile broadband or fixed internet; Q-commerce real-time tracking, demand forecasting, and delivery management all run on mobile connectivity. Second, digital advertising from Internet Platforms — SE04 retail and consumer brands buy digital advertising inventory from SE09 search, social, and content platforms to reach consumers. High strength — e-commerce is structurally impossible without internet connectivity; digital advertising is the primary consumer marketing channel across EM markets.

SE04 has two distinct electricity dependencies on SE10. First, industrial/commercial electricity — automotive manufacturing plants, consumer electronics assembly facilities, textile mills, retail stores, hotels, restaurants, cinemas, and data centres underpinning e-commerce platforms all consume grid electricity as a non-negotiable operational input. Manufacturing operations are energy-intensive and cannot operate without continuous power supply. Second, EV charging — the EV sub-segment creates a direct electricity dependency as EV vehicles require charging infrastructure connected to the SE10 grid. High strength — manufacturing cannot operate without electricity; the ICE fuel dependency (SE01) and EV charging dependency (SE10) together constitute the full vehicle energy value chain.

SE04 buys real estate from SE11 across two structural categories. First, retail space — organised retail brands (fashion, F&B, entertainment, consumer electronics) lease Grade A mall space and high-street retail locations from SE11 Retail and Mixed-Use Real Estate developers and REITs. Retail brand store rollout is entirely dependent on access to quality retail real estate — a retailer cannot open stores without physical premises. Second, hotel property — hotel operators frequently operate on a lease or management contract basis from hotel asset owners classified in SE11 Specialty Real Estate. High strength — retail brand operations cannot exist without physical store locations; hotel operations require physical property access.

SE04 hospitality, travel, and retail sub-sectors depend on SE12 transport infrastructure for customer access — airports, highways, and port/cruise infrastructure are physical prerequisites for tourism and retail destination viability. Hotels in tier-II/III cities are economically justified only when airport connectivity or highway access exists. Mall and retail park viability is directly linked to road infrastructure quality and public transit access in catchment areas. Medium strength — infrastructure access is a precondition for business models but is not an ongoing operational input cost.

SE05 has two distinct energy dependencies on SE01. First, household cooking fuel — LPG is the primary clean transitional cooking fuel across EM households, replacing biomass and kerosene. Government-supported distribution programmes have driven mass LPG adoption across diverse EM geographies: subsidy-based household connection programmes in India, national kerosene-to-LPG conversion programmes in Indonesia, market-driven distribution networks in Brazil and Latin America, and government-supported rollout in Africa. Second, food processing energy — FMCG and food processing companies use natural gas and coal for industrial process heat in their manufacturing operations. Cold chain logistics for dairy, meat, and perishables relies on diesel from SE01.

SE05 buys from SE02 across three distinct categories. First, agrochemicals and fertilisers — SE05 agricultural upstream depends on SE02 fertilisers (urea, DAP, NPK) and agrochemicals (pesticides, herbicides, fungicides) as essential crop production inputs. Crop production without these inputs sees material yield reduction — the dependency is structurally non-substitutable. Second, packaging materials — FMCG, food processing, dairy, and beverage companies rely on flexible packaging (polymer films, laminates, pouches), paperboard cartons, corrugated boxes, and rigid packaging from SE02 paper, packaging, and petrochemical sub-industries. Third, specialty chemicals for formulation — household products and personal care manufacturers buy specialty chemicals from SE02 as the functional raw materials in their formulations: surfactants for detergents, fragrance chemicals, emulsifiers, preservatives, and UV filters for personal care and cosmetics.

SE05 buys from SE03 across two critical categories. First, logistics and distribution services — FMCG and food companies depend fundamentally on SE03 freight and logistics sub-industries for product distribution across dispersed retail networks. Perishable categories require cold chain logistics as a mandatory, non-substitutable operational requirement: cold chain failure renders perishable product unsaleable. FMCG supply chains are among the most logistics-intensive in the economy — high SKU count, dispersed geography, frequent replenishment cycles, and time-sensitive freshness requirements create structural dependence on SE03 logistics. Second, agricultural machinery — the farming upstream of SE05 food production requires capital equipment from SE03 agricultural machinery sub-industries.

FMCG companies (SE05) are structurally the largest buyers of advertising inventory from SE04 Media and Entertainment platforms. FMCG brands are the structurally non-substitutable revenue source for television broadcasting (GECs) and digital/OTT platforms — GEC TV channels are sustained by FMCG advertising budgets. FMCG products require mass consumer reach and high frequency of exposure to build and maintain brand recall, making mass media advertising a structural business requirement, not a discretionary spend. High strength — FMCG pullback in advertising directly impairs SE04 media platform revenues.

SE05 has two SE07 dependencies. First, agricultural credit — commercial banks and development finance institutions provide agricultural working capital loans to farmers for crop production; in most EM geographies, public sector banks are the primary channel for formal agricultural credit, often via government-supported schemes such as India Kisan Credit Card, Brazil Pronaf, or Indonesia KUR. Without institutional agricultural credit, farming sectors in EM economies revert to informal moneylenders at prohibitive rates. Second, crop insurance — government-backed crop insurance schemes covering farmers against weather and yield risk are a universal feature of EM agricultural policy across India, Brazil, China, and Africa; co-delivered through the banking and insurance system, with premiums subsidised by government.

SE05 FMCG and food companies buy GenAI platforms, AI supply chain tools, and digital commerce infrastructure from SE08. GenAI for demand forecasting and route planning, AI-driven order management systems, digital commerce platforms, AI for anti-counterfeiting, personalisation engines for FMCG distributors. In food processing: Manufacturing Execution Systems, laboratory information management, and ERP for procurement and supply chain. Medium strength — FMCG supply chains are increasingly IT-dependent for efficiency, but physical product manufacturing and distribution can operate at reduced efficiency without advanced IT.

SE05 has connectivity dependencies across multiple sub-sectors. FMCG companies buy enterprise internet and mobile connectivity for sales force automation, distributor management systems, and real-time trade marketing tools. BharatNet rural fibre connectivity enables farmers to access e-NAM, digital credit, and crop insurance over mobile broadband. FMCG brands also buy digital advertising inventory from SE09 Internet Platforms as a growing share of total advertising spend. Medium strength — FMCG operations can continue without advanced connectivity but distribution efficiency is materially impaired.

SE05 food processing, dairy, beverage, and FMCG manufacturing operations are significant industrial electricity buyers from SE10. Food processing plants use electricity for processing equipment, conveyor systems, and packaging lines. Dairy pasteurisation, sterilisation, and cold storage require continuous, stable electricity — a power disruption in a dairy plant renders product unsaleable. Beverage bottling lines, carbonation, and refrigeration are electricity-intensive. Cold chain infrastructure throughout SE05 distribution network is electricity-dependent — power outage disrupts the entire perishable supply chain. High strength — food processing and dairy manufacturing cannot operate without continuous electricity; cold chain breaks are irreversible for perishable products.

SE05 FMCG companies, food processors, and dairy companies lease warehousing and cold storage real estate from SE11 Warehousing and Logistics Parks for their distribution networks. FMCG companies require geographically dispersed warehouse facilities (mother warehouses, regional distribution centres, cold stores for dairy and chilled products) to serve dispersed retail networks. Cold storage real estate for dairy and seafood is a dedicated sub-category within SE11 that is structurally essential for those perishable supply chains. Medium strength — FMCG distribution depends on leased warehousing, but the sector can use alternative logistics arrangements; the formal Grade A warehousing dependency is growing as supply chains formalise.

SE05 distribution network depends on SE12 transport infrastructure — roads, highways, rail freight corridors, and port infrastructure — as the physical backbone through which food and consumer goods reach dispersed markets. In EM geographies, road and rail network quality is a primary determinant of FMCG distribution reach: poor road infrastructure raises last-mile delivery costs, increases transit times for perishables, and structurally limits accessible market geography. Port infrastructure enables import of agri-commodities (palm oil, pulses) and export of processed food products. The dependency is infrastructure access, not a direct service purchase — SE12 disruption raises distribution costs and constrains geographic reach.

SE06 hospitals and healthcare facilities consume electricity (primarily from SE10, which in turn buys from SE01) and some direct fuel inputs (diesel for backup generators, medical gases that include industrial gases from SE02). The direct SE01 dependency is low — healthcare primary energy input is electricity (SE10), not direct fuel from SE01. Diesel backup generators are used for power backup but represent a small fraction of operating costs. Worth tracking for cascade completeness — a major SE01 disruption that causes SE10 power cuts would affect hospitals, but the primary cascade path runs SE01 to SE10 to SE06, not SE01 to SE06 directly.

SE06 buys from SE02 across two distinct categories. First, chemical raw material inputs — pharmaceutical manufacturers depend on SE02 specialty chemicals and bulk chemicals for API synthesis: Key Starting Materials (KSMs) and drug intermediates are the building blocks for multi-step API synthesis; specialty chemicals (solvents, reagents, excipients) are consumed throughout the manufacturing process. The dependency is structural and non-substitutable — pharma manufacturing cannot proceed without chemical raw material inputs. EM pharma industries have historically sourced KSMs and API precursors from Chinese and Western chemical suppliers, creating a structural import dependency. Second, manufactured packaging components — SE06 depends on SE02 packaging sub-industries for pharma-grade packaging: glass vials, blister packs, strip packaging, aluminium foil, HDPE bottles, and sterile medical packaging.

SE06 buys from SE03 across three categories. First, pharma cold chain logistics — temperature-controlled distribution of vaccines, biologics, specialty drugs, and insulin is a mandatory regulatory requirement (WHO Good Distribution Practice) throughout the pharmaceutical supply chain. Biologics and biosimilars require strict cold chain maintenance to preserve efficacy and regulatory compliance — disruption of cold chain directly compromises drug safety and viability. Second, hospital EPC construction — private hospital chains are in an active multi-year bed addition programme across EM geographies, requiring EPC construction services from SE03 for hospital building, medical gas piping, HVAC for clean rooms, electrical infrastructure, and medical support systems. Third, medical and healthcare staffing — hospitals are large-scale buyers of temporary and permanent staffing services from SE03 Staffing and Human Capital sub-industry.

SE06 has two SE07 dependencies. First, health insurance — general/non-life insurers including government-mandated health insurance schemes provide retail and group health insurance covering medical expenses. Health insurance is the largest or among the largest non-life insurance segments across most EM geographies. Government health insurance schemes (India PMJAY, Thailand Universal Coverage Scheme, Brazil SUS-linked private complement) cover secondary and tertiary hospitalisation for lower-income populations. Health insurance enables healthcare utilisation — without it, out-of-pocket costs structurally suppress demand for formal healthcare services. Second, hospital and healthcare infrastructure financing — commercial banks and DFIs provide construction finance for hospital buildings, medical equipment finance, and working capital credit. PE/VC is the primary growth equity provider for private hospital chains and diagnostics companies.

SE06 healthcare and life sciences companies buy IT services and AI platforms from SE08 across multiple critical applications: electronic health records (EHR) and hospital management information systems (HMIS) are now standard infrastructure for hospitals; AI platforms for clinical decision support, radiology image analysis, and diagnostic algorithms are transforming care delivery; LLMs fine-tuned on medical data within secure VPC environments for drug discovery and clinical research; telemedicine platforms and digital health apps; pharma companies buy IT for manufacturing execution systems, laboratory information management, and regulatory compliance tracking. High strength — modern hospital operations are IT-dependent; pharma manufacturing compliance requires validated IT systems.

SE06 healthcare sector depends on SE09 connectivity for two growing applications. Telemedicine and digital health — remote diagnosis, teleconsultation, and remote patient monitoring are all delivered over mobile broadband or fixed internet. eSanjeevani telemedicine and equivalent platforms across EM geographies have served large volumes of patient sessions, entirely over mobile and broadband connectivity; this extends to Africa, Southeast Asia, and LatAm where mobile broadband is the primary healthcare access vehicle for underserved populations. Hospital operations — clinical information systems, PACS, electronic health records, and IoT-enabled medical devices require hospital-grade enterprise connectivity. Medium strength — hospital physical operations can continue without connectivity, but digital health delivery is entirely connectivity-dependent.

SE06 is critically dependent on uninterrupted electricity from SE10 across three sub-sectors. First, hospitals — 24/7 uninterrupted power is mandatory for intensive care units, operation theatres, imaging equipment (MRI, CT), laboratory refrigeration, life support systems, and climate control; a power failure in a hospital directly endangers patient lives. Second, pharmaceutical GMP manufacturing — pharma clean rooms, fermentation vessels, centrifuges, autoclave sterilisers, cold storage, and HVAC all require continuous, stable power; GMP compliance requires power conditions within tight tolerances; any power disruption risks batch contamination and regulatory non-compliance. Third, CRDMO laboratories — analytical instruments, cryo-storage for cell lines, and bioreactors for biologics production are energy-intensive and require stable power supply.

SE06 is a significant buyer of real estate from SE11 across two distinct categories. First, hospital campus real estate — private hospital chains building greenfield campuses require land acquisition and construction on SE11 real estate assets; tertiary care hospitals are large-footprint facilities requiring substantial land and purpose-built construction. Private hospital operators account for a structurally significant and growing share of hospital bed capacity across EM healthcare systems. Second, commercial clinical space — outpatient departments, diagnostic labs, and single-specialty clinics increasingly occupy SE11 commercial real estate (retail mall clinic spaces, commercial office park medical suites). High strength — hospital operations are physically anchored to their real estate footprint; healthcare facilities cannot function without physical premises.

SE07 financial institutions (banks, insurance companies, asset managers, exchanges) consume electricity for data centres, office operations, and branch networks. The direct SE01 dependency is low — SE07 is not energy-intensive in the way that manufacturing sectors are. Its electricity comes primarily via SE10. The direct relationship with SE01 is limited to diesel for backup generation in data centres and office buildings. Worth tracking for cascade completeness in the context of rapidly expanding financial sector data centres, which are becoming significant electricity consumers.

SE03 BPO sub-industry serves SE07 Financials as its single largest end market. Financial institutions across all EM geographies outsource non-core back-office operations to SE03 BPO providers: insurance claim processing, mortgage document verification, trade settlement back-office, KYC/AML data processing, credit card disputes, and call centre customer service. India is the world leading BPO hub with SE07 BFSI as its largest vertical. The SE03 BPO relationship to SE07 is the reverse of most SE07 capital flow relationships — here SE07 is the buyer of SE03 services. Medium strength — financial institutions can re-insource or switch BPO providers, but the cost efficiency of SE03 BPO is structurally embedded in SE07 operating models.

BFSI companies (banks, insurers, NBFCs, fintechs) are significant buyers of advertising from SE04 media platforms — motor insurance, home loans, credit cards, investment products, and digital payments all require mass consumer marketing. BFSI advertising spend has been growing across digital, TV, and print formats as financial products move toward direct consumer acquisition. Financial services sector IT spending is growing rapidly as institutions compete on digital capabilities and regulatory requirements mandate modern infrastructure. SE07 fintech, digital banking, and payments infrastructure operates on SE09 mobile connectivity as its physical delivery layer. SE07 digital payments infrastructure requires continuous, low-latency mobile network availability to process transactions in real time. High strength — digital financial inclusion agenda (UPI, digital lending for the unbanked) is structurally dependent on mobile connectivity; without SE09 network coverage, financial services cannot reach a significant proportion of the population.

SE07 financial institutions buy electricity from SE10 for data centres, office operations, ATM networks, and branch infrastructure. Data centres supporting core banking, trading systems, and payment processing are significant electricity consumers — a power outage at a financial sector data centre is an operational emergency. Office buildings and branch networks consume electricity for lighting, HVAC, and computing. The dependency is medium — financial services have robust backup power (UPS, diesel generators) for short outages and can absorb brief interruptions without operational failure; extended grid outages would be more disruptive but the sector is resilient by design.

SE07 financial institutions are significant occupiers of commercial real estate — bank branches across dispersed retail networks, insurance company offices, NBFC regional offices, AMC headquarters and distribution offices, stock exchange facilities, and financial data centres all require physical premises from SE11. Commercial real estate provides the physical operating infrastructure for SE07 branch and office network across EM geographies. The dependency is low because real estate is an operational overhead for SE07, not a primary input to its core financial intermediation function. A major real estate market disruption raises occupancy costs for SE07 but does not impair its core credit or insurance operations.

SE08 data centres and IT campuses are rapidly growing and structurally significant buyers of electricity from SE01/SE10. AI workloads are driving hyperscale data centre buildout at a pace that is making data centres one of the largest and fastest-growing new categories of electricity demand globally — at projected scale, AI data centres could consume a structurally significant share of total national electricity generation in major markets. In cascade terms: SE01 disruption causes SE10 curtailment causing SE08 data centre operational risk.

SE08 buys from SE02 across two categories. First, rare earth elements, critical minerals, and specialty chemicals — semiconductor fabrication and ESDM manufacturing require REEs (neodymium, dysprosium, terbium for chip motors and magnets), specialty photoresists and etchants, ultra-pure process gases, and silicon wafers as direct fabrication inputs. Second, structural materials for data centre and ESDM construction — copper (for PCBs, power distribution busbars, cable interconnects, and liquid cooling infrastructure), aluminium (for heat sinks, chassis, rack structures), and steel (for building infrastructure). High strength — semiconductor-grade REEs and specialty chemicals are non-substitutable inputs; disruption halts fabrication.

SE08 IT companies buy facilities management, security services, and logistics from SE03. First, IT parks and GCC campuses require professional facilities management (FM) services — housekeeping, security guards, cafeteria operations, building maintenance, and ground transport. Second, hardware logistics — SE03 logistics operators handle last-mile delivery of IT hardware, servers, and networking equipment to data centres and enterprise clients. Third, construction services for greenfield IT campus development. Medium strength — IT operations depend on FM and logistics services but these are commodity services with multiple providers; not production-critical in the way that electricity or internet bandwidth are.

SE08 IT companies receive both PE/VC growth equity and public market capital from SE07 capital markets sub-industries. PE/VC is the primary funding source for technology startups and scale-ups — technology consistently ranks among the top three PE investment sectors across all major EM geographies (India, Brazil, China, Southeast Asia). Investment banking facilitates technology company IPOs and follow-on equity raises — technology IPOs have been a structurally significant driver of primary equity market activity in EM capital markets. Asset management channels institutional investor capital into technology equity. The dependency is high because the technology sector growth trajectory in EM markets is funded primarily through equity capital from SE07.

SE08 IT services, GCCs, cloud infrastructure, and data centre operations are entirely dependent on SE09 connectivity. IT services companies and GCCs buy enterprise internet bandwidth (leased lines, MPLS, SD-WAN) from telecom operators for connecting offshore delivery centres to client networks globally. Cloud and data centre operators require high-capacity internet connectivity from national and international internet exchanges and submarine cable connectivity to serve cloud tenants and CDN delivery. SE08 internet platforms and cloud services are physically delivered over SE09 network infrastructure. The dependency is structural and non-substitutable: SE08 cloud services, IT delivery, and digital platforms cannot function without high-bandwidth, low-latency connectivity from SE09.

SE08 is the single largest commercial real estate tenant sector — across two distinct asset types. First, Grade A office space — GCCs and IT services companies are structurally dominant office space absorbers; purpose-built IT parks and SEZs have been constructed specifically to serve the IT and GCC tenant base. The IT and GCC sector has consistently been the largest driver of Grade A office leasing. Second, data centre real estate — hyperscale data centres occupy SE11 Data Centre Real Estate assets; major hyperscale campuses are SE11 assets occupied by SE08 operators. High strength — IT and GCC operations are physically anchored to their office footprint; data centre infrastructure is immovable once built.

SE09 telecom operators and tower companies buy energy from SE01 across two channels. First, diesel for tower backup generators — towers in areas without reliable grid power (rural EM markets, Africa, Southeast Asia) run on diesel generators as primary or backup power; diesel procurement from SE01 downstream is a direct operational cost for tower operators in these markets. Second, LPG/gas for office and facility heating in colder EM markets. The dependency is medium — in urban markets with reliable grid, SE09 primarily buys electricity from SE10 not direct fuel from SE01; the diesel dependency is significant in rural/off-grid tower deployments but declining as solar+battery replaces diesel generators in green telecom programmes.

SE09 buys structural materials from SE02 for tower construction and fibre infrastructure deployment. Steel is the primary structural material for telecom tower fabrication (lattice towers, monopoles, rooftop structures). Copper was historically used for last-mile access loops but is being replaced by fibre; copper remains in use for legacy access networks and some tower components. Optical fibre cables use specialty glass and polymer materials from SE02 specialty chemicals and materials sub-industries. With hundreds of thousands of active tower sites across EM geographies and ongoing 5G densification requiring additional towers and small cells, SE09 structural material procurement from SE02 is ongoing and growing. Medium strength — tower steel is a capital input for network expansion, not an ongoing operational input.

SE09 telecom operators buy tower construction and field maintenance services from SE03. Tower civil construction (foundation, tower fabrication and erection, power systems installation) is procured from SE03 civil contractors. Field maintenance services (preventive and corrective maintenance of tower sites) use SE03 field service companies. Optical fibre cable laying for BharatNet and enterprise connectivity requires civil trenching and duct installation from SE03 civil contractors. Low strength — these are periodic capital and maintenance expenditures, not ongoing operational inputs; SE09 network operations can continue without new tower construction.

Telecom operators are significant buyers of advertising from SE04 media platforms — plan promotions, 5G service launches, broadband offerings, and digital service bundles require large-scale consumer marketing across TV, OTT, and digital. Telecom devotes a structurally high proportion of its advertising budget to digital, reflecting the digital-first nature of telecom customer acquisition. Telecom operators have also created direct platform partnerships and captive media assets which reduce but do not eliminate reliance on third-party media inventory. Medium strength — telecom advertising is material but the existence of captive media platforms means this relationship is less structurally locked than FMCG dependency on third-party mass media.

SE09 telecom operators and tower companies raise significant debt capital from SE07 for spectrum acquisition, network expansion, and tower infrastructure financing. Spectrum auctions require immediate large payments which telecom operators finance through deferred spectrum payment bonds and long-term bank credit — this is a universal pattern across EM telecom markets (India, Brazil, Indonesia, Africa). Tower InvITs and tower infrastructure companies raise infrastructure debt from bond markets facilitated by SE07 investment banking and fixed income intermediaries. The dependency is medium — SE09 raises capital from SE07 but has some ability to generate internal cash flows and the relationship is less existential than the high-strength dependencies in SE01/SE02/SE03.

SE09 buys from SE08 across two categories. First, AI and software services — telecom operators buy AI platforms for autonomous network management, OSS/BSS modernisation, AI-powered customer service automation, agentic AI for self-optimising network performance, and analytics for churn prediction and ARPU optimisation. Second, network equipment and components — telecom operators buy communications and networking equipment (routers, switches, RAN equipment) from SE08 Communications and Networking Equipment manufacturers; also ESDM-manufactured electronic components for network hardware. High strength — modern telecom networks cannot manage 5G complexity without AI; network equipment procurement is non-negotiable for network operation.

SE09 buys electricity from SE10 as the primary and dominant operational cost for its tower and network infrastructure. Tower electricity — each active telecom tower site consumes continuous power for active RAN equipment, air conditioning, and battery backup systems; with hundreds of thousands of towers operating across EM geographies, aggregate electricity consumption is substantial. Tower operators run green telecom programmes (rooftop solar, lithium-ion battery backup) to reduce grid dependency, but grid electricity remains the primary supply source. High strength — telecom towers cannot maintain network uptime without continuous power supply; power disruption at tower sites directly creates coverage outages affecting all customers and services in the affected geography.

SE09 telecom operators and tower infrastructure companies lease physical site space — rooftop locations, ground-level plots, and building access rights — from SE11 Specialty Real Estate (telecom tower REITs and individual property owners). Every telecom tower requires a physical site with power and access rights. Tower tenancy agreements between telecom operators (SE09) and site owners (SE11) are structured as long-duration leases (typically 15-30 years). The tower REIT model is precisely the SE11 asset ownership + SE09 operator tenancy structure. Medium strength — telecom networks cannot operate without physical tower sites, but in EM markets telecom companies often own some towers outright while leasing others.

SE09 depends on SE12 transport and urban infrastructure for two critical access requirements. First, fibre network right-of-way — laying optical fibre cables requires access to road corridors, highway shoulders, railway tracks, and urban utility ducts; SE12 road/rail infrastructure operators grant right-of-way licences to telecom operators for fibre duct installation; BharatNet rural fibre rollout specifically uses railway track corridors for long-haul fibre routing. Second, tower infrastructure access — tower sites at highways, airports, and urban transport nodes require SE12 infrastructure operator permission and access agreements. Medium strength — right-of-way is a structural requirement for network expansion and densification, but existing RoW licences provide continuity.

SE10 buys from SE01 across two distinct categories. First, energy fuel — conventional power generation is structurally dependent on thermal coal and natural gas as primary generation fuels. Coal-based thermal power is the dominant generation source in most coal-producing EM economies. In many EM geographies the natural gas component arrives as LNG via SE12 port infrastructure rather than domestic pipeline, adding a second-order infrastructure dependency. Second, capital equipment — utility-scale renewable power operators procure solar PV modules and cells from SE01 IG0103 renewable equipment manufacturing sub-sector. The two natures are structurally separate — conventional generation drives the energy dependency, renewable generation drives the capital/component procurement dependency.

SE10 buys from SE02 across two distinct categories. First, structural materials — SE10 transmission and distribution companies are direct buyers of structural steel for transmission tower fabrication, HVDC line structures, and substation civil works; copper for transformer windings, HV cable conductors, and distribution wiring; and aluminium conductors (ACSR) for transmission lines. Domestic CRGO electrical steel supply for transformer cores does not meet demand in most EM geographies — a structural bottleneck that constrains grid expansion and forces import dependence. Second, specialty chemicals — thermal power plants are direct buyers of water treatment chemicals (scale inhibitors, corrosion inhibitors, biocides, boiler feedwater treatment chemicals, cooling tower chemicals) for operational maintenance.

SE10 buys from SE03 across three categories. First, power generation equipment — gas turbines, steam turbines, hydro turbines, transformer equipment, switchgear, and balance-of-plant equipment from SE03 heavy electrical equipment manufacturers. Second, civil construction and EPC services — power plant construction, substation civil works, transmission tower erection, and distribution network expansion are all procured from SE03 EPC contractors. Third, agricultural equipment linkage — agricultural irrigation pumps and rural electrification infrastructure connect SE10 distribution to SE05 agricultural water pumping loads. High strength — power plant commissioning and grid expansion physically cannot occur without SE03 equipment and EPC services.

SE10 power sector is consistently the largest sub-segment of SE07 infrastructure project finance book across EM geographies. Power generation — both conventional and renewable — requires long-tenor project finance from commercial banks, development finance institutions (DFIs), and bond markets. DFIs dedicated to infrastructure (India NaBFID, Brazil BNDES, Indonesia PT Sarana Multi Infrastruktur, IFC/ADB for multilateral flows) provide concessional and patient capital for power sector development. Green bonds and sustainability-linked loans are increasingly the funding route for renewable energy capacity. Without SE07 capital, national renewable energy targets and the broader power sector expansion programmes that EM economies require cannot be financed.

SE10 buys IT systems and digital services from SE08 across two primary categories. First, operational technology — SCADA and Distribution Management Systems (DMS) deployed by power distribution utilities for network control and loss reduction; smart metering infrastructure deployed under grid modernisation programmes; Energy Management Systems (EMS) and Wide Area Monitoring Systems (WAMS) for transmission operators; grid integration analytics and demand forecasting software for renewable integration management. Second, enterprise IT — ERP, billing systems, and customer relationship platforms for utilities. The dependency is medium: the physical grid can operate without advanced IT but suboptimally; as grids become more complex with renewable integration and two-way power flows, operational IT becomes structurally necessary.

SE10 power utilities buy connectivity from SE09 for smart grid communication and operational monitoring. Smart meter data from millions of distribution points is transmitted over mobile networks (NB-IoT, LTE-M) to DISCOM control centres — smart metering depends on SE09 cellular IoT connectivity for data backhaul. Distribution management systems (DMS) and SCADA networks use wireless and fibre connectivity for real-time grid monitoring and fault detection. Renewable energy plant monitoring in remote locations uses cellular connectivity for generation data telemetry. Medium strength — grid operations predate digital connectivity and can function without it, but smart metering programmes and SCADA modernisation are making cellular connectivity structurally embedded in distribution operations.

SE10 transmission operators depend on SE12 infrastructure corridors — land rights-of-way, transmission corridors, and associated civil infrastructure — for grid expansion. Transmission network expansion is materially constrained by right-of-way acquisition, land clearances, and multi-agency approvals that are effectively SE12 infrastructure access issues. Renewable energy evacuation from solar/wind-rich states is directly gated on corridor availability. The dependency is infrastructure access, not raw material or capital — SE12 disruption constrains grid expansion pace rather than current operations.

SE11 real estate operators buy energy inputs from SE01 across two categories. First, diesel for backup power generators in commercial buildings, data centre real estate, and residential backup systems — a direct SE01 to SE11 relationship for properties in EM markets with unreliable grid power. Second, LPG/PNG for cooking in residential projects and hospitality properties, and for industrial heating in logistics parks and cold storage facilities. The dependency is low — real estate as a sector is primarily an electricity buyer (SE10) not a direct fossil fuel buyer; the diesel and gas dependencies are operational overheads rather than structural production inputs.

SE11 construction and real estate is the single largest end-market for SE02 construction materials sub-industries. Cement is the primary binding material for all residential, commercial, and industrial construction. Steel (TMT bars, structural steel) provides tensile strength in reinforced concrete structures. Glass is used in facades, windows, and interior finishes. Paints and coatings are applied at the finishing stage of construction. Building products (ceramic tiles, sanitary ware, plywood/MDF) are used throughout construction. Demand for SE02 construction materials is directly correlated with housing starts, commercial construction activity, and infrastructure project awards.

SE11 real estate developers buy EPC construction services and building products from SE03 for physical construction of all real estate asset types. Residential development requires civil construction, structural engineering, MEP works, and building products installation. Commercial office and retail construction requires specialised fit-out services. Data centre construction requires precision electrical and cooling system installation. Hospital and specialty real estate construction requires medical gas piping, clean room HVAC, and radiation shielding. SE03 EPC contractors build the asset and hand it over to SE11 developers/operators. High strength — real estate development is physically impossible without SE03 construction services.

SE11 is structurally dependent on SE07 in two ways. First, home loans — housing finance markets across EM geographies are among the fastest-growing segments of the credit system, reflecting the structural housing deficit relative to urbanisation rates; commercial banks and Housing Finance Companies provide the mortgage credit that enables residential real estate demand. Without home loans, residential housing demand would collapse to cash buyers only. Second, construction finance — developers receive construction loans from banks and NBFCs to fund project development before sale proceeds arrive. Commercial real estate credit for offices, logistics parks, data centres is also a structurally large SE07 to SE11 capital flow, enabling the Grade A real estate stock that corporate tenants require.

SE11 real estate operators and developers buy IT services and PropTech solutions from SE08 for asset management and operational efficiency. Applications include: AI-driven building energy management systems; IoT-enabled predictive maintenance platforms; digital permitting and approval systems; AI-based tenant screening and lease management platforms; real estate analytics and market intelligence tools; construction technology platforms for project monitoring. Green building certification compliance often requires IT-based energy monitoring systems. Medium strength — real estate assets can operate without advanced IT but at higher operating costs and lower tenant satisfaction; IT adoption is being driven by ESG compliance requirements from institutional tenants and global investors.

SE11 buys electricity from SE10 across two structurally distinct categories. First, data centre real estate — electricity is the dominant operating cost for data centres, accounting for the substantial majority of total DC operating expenses. Data centre operators purchase electricity either from distribution utilities under commercial tariffs or directly from renewable generators under power purchase agreements. Data centre power demand is growing rapidly as AI workloads drive higher rack density requirements. Second, general real estate operations — commercial office buildings, shopping malls, residential complexes, and warehousing facilities all consume electricity for lighting, HVAC, lifts, security systems, and common area operations. High strength overall — data centres cannot operate without continuous high-grade power supply.

SE11 data centre real estate has a structural dependency on SE12 connectivity infrastructure — high-capacity fibre networks, submarine cable landing stations, and national long-distance connectivity backbone are prerequisites for data centre viability. Data centres are not viable without reliable, high-bandwidth internet connectivity to serve cloud, colocation, and enterprise clients. Site selection for hyperscale and colocation facilities is directly gated on proximity to fibre infrastructure and submarine cable landing points. Broader SE11 real estate also depends on SE12 road and transport infrastructure for property access — real estate developments in new corridors are viable only after highway or metro connectivity is established. Medium strength — connectivity infrastructure is a site selection prerequisite and value driver but the dependency is on existing infrastructure, not ongoing operational services.

SE12 transport infrastructure operators buy energy inputs from SE01 across two primary uses. First, bitumen — a refinery heavy-end product from SE01 downstream refining is the primary road surfacing material for flexible pavement construction; bitumen price spikes directly compress road developer and concessionaire margins. Second, aviation turbine fuel — airports facilitate ATF sales to airlines and consume diesel for ground equipment and backup power. Rail electrification reduces diesel dependency for SE12 rail operators, but road and airport sub-sectors remain energy-dependent. Medium strength — SE12 infrastructure assets are long-lived and the energy relationship is largely at the construction and maintenance phase rather than throughput operations.

SE12 transport infrastructure asset owners and operators depend on SE02 for the physical materials used in construction of roads, highways, ports, and waterways. Steel is used extensively in bridge construction, flyovers, rail structures, and port handling equipment. Cement is the primary material for road sub-base, concrete pavement, and port construction. Bitumen (a petrochemical derivative from SE01 via SE02 downstream) is used for road surfacing. Critical minerals and metals are increasingly required for smart infrastructure (sensors, electronics). The B2G end market dominates as most infrastructure is government-funded or PPP.

SE12 infrastructure asset developers buy EPC construction services and capital equipment from SE03 for physical construction of all transport and urban infrastructure asset types. Roads and highways require civil construction services and road-building machinery. Ports require marine construction, dredging, crane equipment, and container handling systems. Airports require terminal construction, runway works, and specialised aviation ground equipment. Rail infrastructure requires track-laying machinery, signalling systems, and rolling stock components. The dependency is high — infrastructure assets cannot be built without SE03 EPC and equipment; SE12 is structurally the largest single buyer of SE03 EPC services by project value in most EM economies.

SE12 infrastructure asset developers and InvITs depend on SE07 for long-tenor project finance, infrastructure bonds, and InvIT unit subscriptions. Infrastructure credit consistently represents the largest single share of industrial credit in most EM banking systems — power, roads, ports, and rail collectively absorb a structural portion of total bank credit. DFIs provide construction-phase project loans at tenors that commercial banks cannot match. Once assets are operational, infrastructure InvITs refinance construction loans with long-term bond market capital. Asset management channels retail and institutional investor savings into InvIT units. Life insurers invest in infrastructure bonds as long-duration liability-matching assets. The scale of EM infrastructure investment needs far exceeds government balance sheet capacity in most geographies.

SE12 buys IT services and digital platforms from SE08 across transport and urban infrastructure applications. First, port digitalisation — port operators buy digital twin platforms, IoT sensor networks, AI-driven berth allocation systems, cloud-based just-in-time vessel arrival systems, and port community systems from SE08. Second, transport management systems — toll road operators buy electronic tolling infrastructure (FASTag/RFID systems, national electronic toll collection platforms), traffic management systems, and vehicle classification systems from SE08. Third, urban and smart city IT — urban infrastructure operators buy integrated command and control centre (ICCC) platforms, traffic signal management, CCTV networks, and digital governance systems. Medium strength — infrastructure assets can operate without advanced IT but at significantly lower efficiency.

SE12 infrastructure operators buy connectivity from SE09 for intelligent transport and urban infrastructure systems. Toll road operators use cellular connectivity for FASTag/RFID electronic toll collection, vehicle classification, and ANPR camera data transmission. Port operators buy connectivity for vessel tracking, terminal operating systems, IoT crane monitoring, and gate automation. Airport operators use connectivity for passenger flow management, baggage tracking, and ATC data links. Metro rail and DFC systems use cellular and fibre connectivity for train control, signalling, and passenger information systems. Smart city infrastructure (ICCC platforms, traffic signals, CCTV) is entirely connectivity-dependent. Medium strength — infrastructure operations can continue in degraded mode without advanced connectivity but operational efficiency, safety monitoring, and revenue collection (tolling) are materially impaired.

SE12 infrastructure operators buy electricity from SE10 for operational requirements across all asset types. Airport terminal operations (air conditioning, lighting, passenger processing systems, baggage systems) are major electricity consumers — large international airports consume electricity at industrial scale. Metro rail systems are entirely electrically powered — overhead electrification draws from SE10 grid and is the primary operational energy input. Port crane operations, container terminal equipment, cold storage at ports, and refrigerated warehousing are electricity-intensive. Electronic toll collection infrastructure, traffic management systems, and smart city command centres all require continuous power supply. Medium strength — infrastructure assets have backup power (generators) for critical operations, but ongoing grid electricity is the primary and most cost-efficient supply.

E&P operators contract oilfield services companies for drilling, well completion, seismic surveys, production optimisation, and well intervention services across exploration, development, and production phases. Oilfield services cost inflation is explicitly identified as the primary controllable cost lever for E&P operators, with mature late-life asset production costs running significantly higher than younger assets due in part to elevated services procurement costs.

Crude oil and natural gas produced at wellheads and field gathering systems enter the trunk pipeline and storage terminal network operated by midstream entities for onward movement to refineries and city gate offtake points. This is the first link in the SE01 internal oil & gas chain — E&P output can only reach refineries and end consumers via midstream infrastructure.

E&P operators contract EPC firms for engineering, procurement, and construction of oilfield surface facilities, offshore platforms, pipeline manifolds, and gas processing plants associated with exploration and production operations. This is a service procurement — EPC contractors are engaged for project delivery of upstream hydrocarbon infrastructure on a lump-sum or cost-plus contract basis.

Refineries receive crude oil delivered via trunk crude pipelines and coastal import terminals operated by midstream entities, as the primary refinery feedstock; finished petroleum products flow back into midstream product pipelines for onward distribution to marketing depots. This is the second link in the SE01 internal chain — the refinery is the transformation node between midstream crude delivery and downstream product distribution.

Marketing entities receive the full slate of finished petroleum products — petrol, diesel, ATF, LPG, bitumen, petcoke, naphtha — from refineries and distribute them through retail outlets, aviation fuel stations, LPG distributors, and bulk industrial supply channels. This is a component procurement — finished petroleum products are the physical goods that marketing entities stock and distribute, with refinery gate price as the primary cost input for marketing operations.

Refineries procure natural gas from LNG terminals as process fuel for furnace firing and steam generation across crude distillation, hydrotreating, and reforming units, and as feedstock for Steam Methane Reforming to produce hydrogen for hydroprocessing operations. This is an energy procurement — natural gas is consumed as process fuel and as chemical feedstock for hydrogen production within refinery operations.

Refinery operators supply surplus naphtha — a mid-distillate cut from crude oil distillation — to petrochemical steam crackers as primary feedstock for producing ethylene, propylene, and other olefins; LPG and ethane are secondary feedstocks from the same refinery output.

City gas distribution entities procure LPG supplied by OMC marketing networks as a residential and commercial fuel distributed through cylinder chains, and receive gas allocated through the APM pricing framework that flows via marketing infrastructure at city gate level. This is the final link in the SE01 internal oil & gas chain — the city gas operator sits downstream of the OMC marketing layer for LPG and regulated gas allocation.

OMC marketing entities procure Sustainable Aviation Fuel and liquid biofuels from bioenergy producers for blending into the conventional ATF and biodiesel distribution channel at airport fuel stations and retail outlets; OMC marketing is the primary commercial intermediary between SAF producers and airline end-consumers.

Trunk pipeline operators receive regasified LNG from import terminals and carry it through the national gas grid to industrial consumers, power plants, fertiliser facilities, and CGD city gate stations; IN010202 Midstream is the physical carrier that integrates LNG import supply into the domestic gas network.

City gas distribution networks procure regasified LNG from import terminals as the primary gas supply source when domestic APM gas allocation is insufficient; LNG imports account for approximately one-quarter of India's total gas demand and supply the CGD city gate directly where domestic pipeline gas does not reach.

Coal producers book rake capacity from Indian Railways and pay freight charges for moving coal from mine-heads to power plants, steel plants, and industrial consumers; coal constitutes the dominant share of Indian Railway freight traffic by volume, making it the single most rail-dependent commodity in the Indian economy.

Coal producers and thermal power plants pay freight charges to rail infrastructure operators for bulk coal movement — coal constitutes more than 40% of Indian Railways' total traffic volume and revenue, making it the single most structurally important freight commodity on the rail network. Dedicated freight corridor infrastructure has been specifically designed and constructed to handle industrial bulk freight with coal as the anchor commodity. This is a fee-for-capacity relationship — coal producers and thermal power plants pay per-tonne freight tariffs to rail operators for the right to move coal through the rail network, a relationship reinforced by the coal sector's inability to substitute rail efficiently for bulk commodity movement at scale.

Integrated oil and gas companies procure solar power from utility-scale solar generators via Power Purchase Agreements to supply daytime operational electricity for refineries and terminals, reducing grid electricity costs and Scope 2 emissions under corporate decarbonisation commitments. This is an energy procurement — solar power is procured as a lower-cost operational energy input replacing grid electricity during generation hours.

Integrated oil and gas companies procure wind power from utility-scale wind generators via Power Purchase Agreements to supply round-the-clock operational electricity for coastal refineries and terminals, complementing solar procurement where wind resources are stronger and more consistent. This is an energy procurement — wind power is procured as a lower-cost operational energy input contributing to refinery and terminal baseload energy requirements.

Utility-scale solar project developers procure Battery Energy Storage Systems co-located with generation assets to shift daytime solar generation to evening peak demand periods, reduce curtailment, and provide grid ancillary services; BESS co-deployment with solar is increasingly mandatory in new project configurations as grid operators require dispatchable renewable supply. This is a component procurement — BESS is a capital component of the integrated solar project, procured at construction phase from battery manufacturers and system integrators within IN010306.

Solar cell manufacturers within the solar power sub-industry procure silver in the form of metallization paste for screen-printed front and rear electrical contacts on crystalline silicon PV cells; silver paste is the primary conductive interconnect material in TOPCon and HJT cell architectures.

Utility-scale solar project developers contract EPC firms for engineering, procurement, and construction of solar parks — including site grading, module mounting structure fabrication and installation, DC cabling, inverter installation, and grid-connection substation construction. This is a service procurement — EPC contractors are engaged on a fixed-price or lump-sum contract basis as the primary delivery mechanism for solar capacity addition.

Solar IPPs and renewable energy project developers procure green project finance loans and green bonds underwritten by commercial banks for utility-scale solar farm construction and refinancing; green finance for renewable energy is the fastest-growing infrastructure credit category in most EM banking systems.

Utility-scale wind project developers procure Battery Energy Storage Systems co-located with wind generation assets to firm wind output, reduce curtailment during low-demand periods, and enable wind power to bid into dispatchable generation slots; BESS co-deployment is increasingly embedded in new wind project configurations required by grid operators for capacity allocation.
